abstract: Narrative engagement - a state implicating attention as well as emotional and sequential processing - is crucial in contexts ranging from social interaction to education. Yet we still lack an understanding of how narrative contents and listener perceptions relate to the neural responses they elicit. In this study, we investigate relationships between auditory narratives and listener responses using electroencephalography inter-subject correlation (EEG-ISC), a measure of neural synchrony that has been shown to correlate with narrative cohesion, attention, preference, and learning. We analyzed dense-array EEG recorded from 46 adult participants who listened to social and non-social narrated literary excerpts. The data were spatially optimized using Reliable Components Analysis, and ISC was calculated for each of the three maximally reliable components (RCs) on a per-stimulus basis. While we found no significant relationships between EEG-ISC and broad social/non-social categorizations of the excerpts, ISC for high sociocognitive word usage significantly exceeded that of medium and low word usage in the third spatial component, RC3. We further observed a significant positive correlation between participants' summed ratings of interest, compulsion, and enjoyment and ISC, both for RC2 and when summed across RC1-RC3. Interaction analyses suggest that passage content and behavioral responses contributed independently as additive effects to these relationships. Taken together, these findings extend previous research utilizing EEG-ISC in natural speech contexts and, importantly, suggest that the decomposition of EEG into maximally correlated spatial components can separate co-occurring neural processes engaged during story listening.
